School counsellor's note, Class 10, Thursday.
Ganga came to see me today, very quietly. She is not being bullied, she said. “Nobody does anything to me. That's the problem. I'm just not there for them.”
She described the class group chat where plans are made she's never tagged in, a birthday picnic she saw only in photos, and the walk to the bus stop where her old friend Keerthana now walks ahead with others.
Then she asked, “Is something wrong with me? Maybe I'm boring.”
I told her clearly that being left out does not mean something is wrong with her. We talked about one club she might join. I'll meet her again Monday, and with her permission, I'll speak to her class teacher about mixing groups for projects.

qa.q: Who used to walk with Ganga to the bus stop?
qa.a: Her old friend Keerthana.

qa.q: How was Ganga feeling when she asked if something was wrong with her?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, starting to believe the quiet exclusion meant she was boring or wrong.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take, and why are they helpful?
qa.a: The counsellor told her clearly it wasn't her fault, suggested a club, and planned a follow-up and project mixing, so she isn't left alone with it.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see the walks to the bus stop?
qa.a: Keerthana may not have noticed Ganga being left behind, simply drifting towards a new group.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenager who is never invited or waited for, gradually convinced something is wrong with her.

Saturday night
The party photos are up. Everybody from our class was at Tanya's. Everyone except me and maybe two others. I didn't even know there was a party.
It's not like anyone was mean. That's what makes it worse. Nobody told me not to come. They just didn't think of me.
Even Jeevan, who sits with me in tuition, didn't wait after class on Friday. He just walked off with the others, laughing.
I keep looking in the mirror. Is it my face? Do I talk too much? Too little? There must be something.
Mumma asked why I skipped dinner. I said headache. I don't know how to explain being nobody's first thought.
Sarika

qa.a: Sarika feels hurt, invisible and ashamed, starting to believe something is wrong with Sarika personally.

qa.q: How might Jeevan have seen Friday after tuition?
qa.a: He probably didn't think about it, just walking off with the group, unaware of how it felt.

grounding: A teenager writes about being quietly left out of plans and photos, slowly convinced something is wrong with them.

Jomon, you asked why I don't like groups with one boss. Let me tell you. This is your Rashmi aunty, and this is from Class 9.
Our group had a leader, Sheela. Every Monday, she decided who was “in”. If she liked your bag, you were in. If you talked to the wrong girl, you were out, and nobody would sit with you till she said so.
I watched it happen to my friend Mini. For a whole week, Sheela ignored her, and so did everyone. Even me. I was scared I'd be next.
We all behaved perfectly for Sheela. We laughed at her jokes. We gave her our best pens. We were so busy watching her face, we forgot to be friends with each other.
I never stood up to her. That's what I remember most.

qa.q: Who decided who was "in" every Monday?
qa.a: Sheela did.

qa.q: How did young Rashmi feel when Mini was frozen out?
qa.a: She felt scared and anxious that she'd be next, so she ignored Mini too.

qa.q: At what point in the story could young Rashmi have made a different choice?
qa.a: During Mini's week of being ignored, she could have kept sitting with Mini, even if it risked Sheela's favour.

qa.q: How might Mini have felt that week?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and alone, with even her friend Rashmi ignoring her.

grounding: An elder recalls watching a group leader decide who was in favour each week, keeping everyone fearful and obedient, herself included.

Rain poured on the sports camp, and the bus back to school was leaving in ten minutes. Neil, captain of everything, stood at the bus door, deciding who sat at the back with him.
“Farhan, back. Mehul, back. Aman... no, front today.”
Aman's face fell. Last week he'd been at the back every day. Nobody asked Neil why. Everyone just moved where he pointed.
Charu, dripping at the end of the queue, watched them all glance at Neil's face as they passed him, checking. She'd been sent to the front once, for laughing at the wrong joke.
Aman sat alone in the second row, looking out at the rain. Charu hesitated, then sat next to him. From the back, she heard Neil laugh. She didn't turn round.

qa.q: How long before the bus was leaving?
qa.a: It was leaving in ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling as she watched everyone check Neil's face?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a bit afraid, remembering being sent to the front once for laughing at the wrong joke.

qa.q: What did Charu do that weakened Neil's control a little?
qa.a: She sat with Aman, so he wasn't alone, showing that Neil's choices didn't have to decide everyone's.

qa.q: How might Aman have felt being sent to the front?
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and confused, dropped from the back without any reason.

grounding: Shows a peer watching a group leader decide who sits where, keeping everyone anxious, and quietly sitting with the one left out.

subtype: Hierarchies by college, city and money [Observer]
passage:
At the government degree college in the district town, Avni noticed the lines being drawn within a month.
The students from the city, who'd come because they missed cut-offs elsewhere, sat together at the canteen. They spoke English, carried the latest phones and talked about weekend trips. The village students, Simran among them, came by bus, spoke Hindi, and went home straight after class.
In group projects, the city students took the leading roles. Teachers smiled more at their questions. At the college fest, the city group ran the stage.
Nobody said anyone was better. Nobody needed to. Avni, who was somewhere in between, watched Simran answer a hard question perfectly in Hindi one morning, while a city boy smirked and looked at his phone.

qa.q: How did the village students come to college?
qa.a: They came by bus.

qa.q: How did Avni seem to feel watching the city boy smirk?
qa.a: Avni seemed uncomfortable and unsettled, noticing how status markers were quietly sorting people.

qa.q: What could Avni do to cross the lines she has noticed?
qa.a: She could sit with Simran's group, pair with village students in projects, and praise good answers in any language.

qa.q: How might Simran feel when a good answer met a smirk?
qa.a: Simran might feel hurt and discouraged, having answered well but still being looked down on.

grounding: Shows a student noticing a college pecking order based on city background, English fluency and money, sorted without words.

The students from famous schools found each other within a week. They had the same accents and invited each other to country houses. Rosa, from a small town in Spain, laughed at their jokes a beat too late.
In seminars, people listened more when someone spoke with that certain accent. At the society fair, the committee members all seemed to know each other already.
Fatima, from a state school in Leeds, wasn't sure where she fitted. She watched Rosa, sitting alone with her coffee after a seminar where her good point had been ignored, and sat down beside her.

At the software company's internship programme, Vikas noticed it by the second week. The interns from the famous engineering institutes got the new client projects. The others, like Payal from a state college in Indore, got testing and documentation.
Nobody announced it. It just happened. The famous-institute interns lunched with the managers and used first names. Payal and her group ate at the back of the cafeteria.
In the team meeting, Payal suggested a fix for a bug the others had missed. The manager said, “Hmm, let's see,” and moved on. Ten minutes later, an intern from a big institute said nearly the same thing. The manager said, “Great idea.”
Vikas looked at Payal. She was staring at her notebook.

qa.a: A state college in Indore.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when the manager praised the second intern?
qa.a: Vikas felt uncomfortable and troubled by the unfairness, seeing the same idea treated differently because of the college name.

qa.q: What could Vikas do in the next meeting?
qa.a: Vikas could point out that Payal raised the fix first, making sure credit goes to the right person.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt staring at her notebook?
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and invisible, her idea ignored until someone with a bigger college name said it.
